turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Brennan. We'll do the blood pressure and that before the doctor calls you. Grand, just sit yourself there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I'm grand, nurse. I don't know what all the fuss is about, sure.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's not grand at all. The cough has him wrecked, and I'm the one up with him.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure it's only a tickle. You're making a whole drama of it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Right, arm out for me. There we are. Blood pressure is one hundred and fifty-two over eighty-eight.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse is seventy-six, and the oxygen is ninety-seven percent. Temperature's grand, thirty-six point six.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Nothing wrong with me.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The pressure's still up, Da. That's not nothing.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor Walsh will be in in a minute. You can leave the sleeve rolled.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello Michael, Siobhan. Come on in and sit down. What's been going on with you?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, nothing much. A bit of a cough after a cold. I'm grand, really.
[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, it's not nothing. He's been coughing for weeks, a dry yoke, and he won't tell you the half of it.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): A dry cough. How long would you say it's been there, Michael?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of weeks. Three, maybe. Sure it came with the cold.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's longer than that. I'd say six weeks, easy. It started well before he admits.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): It did not. Three weeks at the outside.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the cold itself, the runny nose and the sneezing, is that still about?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah that's gone. A week ago, maybe. Just this tickle left.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any phlegm with the cough, or is it dry the whole way?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Dry. No phlegm at all. I'm not bringing anything up.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fever? Shivers? Feeling hot at night?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Not a bit of it. I'm not sick-sick.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No fever, I'll give him that. But he is up half the night coughing. Hardly sleeps.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is the cough waking you, Michael?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. I sleep grand.
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He does not sleep grand. I'm in the next room and I hear him half the night.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah you're exaggerating now.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any breathlessness, say on the stairs?
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yes. He has to stop halfway up our stairs. Puffed out.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not breathless. I take my time, that's all. She's making a meal of it.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain at all, or a tightness?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I wouldn't call it pain.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, we'll leave that one. What about wheezing, a whistle in the chest?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No wheeze. Lungs are fine.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're on tablets for the high blood pressure. How long have you had that, and what do you actually take?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The high blood pressure, years now. The ramipril I started lately. And the cholesterol one, atorvastatin, twenty milligram at night.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): The ramipril, what dose is on the box?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligram, I'd say. One in the morning.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's not ten. The box in the press says twenty milligram. I hand him the twenty every morning.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Do you? Sure I thought it was the ten. I don't look at the box.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): And are you taking it every morning, as it's written?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Most mornings.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He misses the odd one if I'm at work. I wouldn't swear he's taking it right.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did you actually start the ramipril? After the last visit?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I couldn't tell you the date. A few weeks back. Maybe a month. I don't know.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was after the clinic in town. I can't mind the day either.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): And you reckon the cough came with a cold, not with the tablet?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the cold. The tablet's grand. My brother is on lisinopril years and he never coughed.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Your brother Tommy, yes, lisinopril ten milligram, but that's him, not you.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fair enough, his tablet isn't yours. Anyone else in the house on blood pressure medicine? No, don't mind. How are you feeling in yourself, energy-wise?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm grand. A small bit tired, but sure I'm seventy-two.
[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's more tired than he'll say. Dragging himself around.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not dragging. A small bit tired is all.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the ankles, or of the lips or tongue, since the ramipril?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. Ankles are grand, face is grand.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Let me have a listen to the chest, if you don't mind. Deep breath now.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear. No crackles, no wheeze. Heart sounds are regular enough.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Told you. Nothing in it.

[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): Look, I'm thinking out loud here. A dry cough that hangs on can be the ramipril, even when it feels like the tail of a cold. It could be either. I'm not putting a firm name on the cough today.
[SEG0060] person_3 (CAREGIVER): So you think it's the tablet?
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think it might be. I can't say for certain, not without seeing what happens when we change it. The cold may still be in the mix.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd rather not be changing tablets for a tickle.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): I hear you. Still, the pressure was one hundred and fifty-two over eighty-eight today, so we need something that works and doesn't keep you coughing.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll stop the ramipril. I'll start losartan instead, fifty milligrams, one tablet by mouth in the morning, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Losartan. Right. And I just bin the ramipril?
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, stop it from today. Don't take the two together. Keep the atorvastatin as it is, twenty milligram at night.
[SEG0067] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll sort the box when we get home so he doesn't mix them.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the cough hasn't eased in a fortnight, come back and we'll look again. Otherwise I'll see you in four weeks for a pressure check.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Grand, if I must.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the lips or tongue swell, or you get properly breathless, don't wait, go to the emergency department.
[SEG0071] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll watch him for that.
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): I won't send you for a chest x-ray today. If it's still there at the next visit we might think about it, but not now.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. I hate those places.
[SEG0074] person_1 (NURSE): Will I book the four-week review at the desk on the way out?
[SEG0075] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, please, four weeks with me. And print the losartan script for the chemist.
[SEG0076] person_1 (NURSE): I'll do that now.
[SEG0077] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Does he take the losartan with food or what?
[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning time, with or without food, same time each day if you can. If a dose is missed, just take the next one, don't double up.
[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not going to be fussing over it. It's only a cough.
[SEG0080] person_4 (DOCTOR): I know you think it's small, and it may well settle. I just don't want to leave you on a tablet that might be the cause.
[SEG0081] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Thanks, doctor. I'll make sure he actually comes back.
[SEG0082] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah sure, we'll see. Mind yourselves.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

omissions.text: Ramipril dose was not recorded on the medication itself despite being discussed: patient thought it was 10 mg each morning, but caregiver said the box says 20 mg and she gives him 20 mg every morning.
Ramipril adherence detail missing from the medication record: patient takes it only 'most mornings' and caregiver says he misses doses if she is at work.
Ramipril start timing was stated as a few weeks ago, maybe a month, after the last clinic visit/in town clinic.
Negative finding missing: no shivers and no feeling hot at night were specifically asked and denied.
Possible chest symptom was not captured: patient gave an equivocal response to chest pain/tightness, saying 'sometimes, not really' and that he would not call it pain.
Caregiver-reported symptom detail missing: cough is worse at night/up half the night coughing.
Doctor advised losartan should be taken in the morning with or without food, preferably at the same time each day.
Planned follow-up booking detail missing: four-week review specifically with Doctor Walsh, and nurse to book it/print the losartan prescription.
Real disagreement not recorded: patient attributed the cough to a cold and rejected changing tablets, while doctor thought ramipril might be causing it and advised changing medication.
